site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Critique and validate the end-to-end UX of the Atlas Tutor chat + practice experience with emphasis on the primary settings/privacy flow and adjacent recovery/feedback paths, on both desktop and mobile viewports.
run_plan.summary: Start from index.html’s existing chat state and validate core interactions: subject navigation, chat history/search, head-tools (Steps/Practice/more), composer send flows, and inline feedback/share/copy controls. Then exercise the right-rail practice problem panel including Hint/Solve/Submit/Correct transitions and progress updates. Finally, validate settings/privacy entry points via the ⚙ control, confirming any dialogs/pages, state persistence, and mobile usability.
assumptions: The only known HTML page in the prescan is index.html; settings/privacy likely appears as an in-page dialog or panel launched from the ⚙ button on index.html.
Practice problems and progress are interactive and update within the same page (no separate HTML pages discovered).
All key UI elements observed (search, subjects nav, Steps/Practice toggle, composer, and practice panel) are functional and can be exercised during the run.
risk_hotspots: index.html → ⚙ settings control (ux-4): unclear whether it opens a dialog/panel; needs validation for settings/privacy flow presence and correct focus/escape behavior
index.html → composer send affordances (Cmd+Enter to send; attach 📎; mic 🎤; send arrow →): risk of broken keyboard/microphone/attachment flows or unclear send state
index.html → chat item feedback/tool buttons (👍/👎, Share, Copy, ↻ Try again): risk these are only decorative or fail to update conversation state
index.html → right rail practice panel: Solve→Submit→Correct 3-state toggle (including Hint button behavior) and difficulty pills; risk of state desync and progress bar not updating
index.html → mobile tap targets: multiple small controls flagged (e.g., ⚙ 22x21, ▶ Practice/⌥ Steps widths < guideline, 👍/👎 32x29) likely to impact usability

phases.title: Baseline & navigation sanity (left rail + head tools)
phases.objective: Confirm the primary structure works: subject navigation, chat history grouping, and the sticky head/tools don’t break scrolling or state.
key_checks: Click a Subject in the left rail (e.g., Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra) and verify the conversation/practice context changes or filters as expected
Use Search chats… input to filter existing history; verify results update without losing chat state
Use sticky head-tools: ⌥ Steps, ▶ Practice, and ⋯; verify each changes the UI (steps mode, practice focus, or menu) and returns cleanly
Click a left-rail chat thread under Today / Last 7 days / Earlier and verify the conversation content updates to the selected thread
exit_criteria: At least one subject click, one history thread switch, and one search action are completed with visible state changes
All three head-tools (⌥ Steps / ▶ Practice / ⋯) are validated for correct toggling and non-breaking layout

phases.title: Chat interaction & recovery (composer + response tools)
phases.objective: Validate message sending, composer controls, and response tool affordances including failure recovery (Try again).
key_checks: Send a short message using Cmd+Enter and verify a new assistant reply appears in the conversation viewport
Test suggestion chips (e.g., the visible suggestions row) by clicking at least one and ensuring it pre-fills or sends as designed
Validate composer controls: click attach 📎 and ensure any file input/modal opens (or confirm graceful no-op); click mic 🎤 and ensure permission/state handling is reasonable
After receiving a reply, use 👍 and 👎 on the assistant message and confirm any visual/recorded state change
Use Share ⤴ and Copy 📋 on the assistant message; verify expected share/copy behavior (or clear messaging if unsupported)
Use ↻ Try again and confirm it triggers a new attempt/reply rather than doing nothing
exit_criteria: At least one successful message send (Cmd+Enter) and one recovery action (↻ Try again) are completed with visible conversation updates
Composer attach and mic interactions are validated for either successful behavior or clear, non-breaking failure handling

phases.title: Practice problems flow + progress correctness
phases.objective: Exercise the right-rail practice panel: hinting, 3-state problem lifecycle (Solve→Submit→Correct), and ensure progress bar updates in sync with completed problems.
key_checks: For multiple problems, click Hint and verify the hint reveals/retracts appropriately (and does not break Solve/Sumbit states)
For at least one problem per difficulty tier visible (EASY/Medium/Hard), run the full lifecycle: Solve → Submit → Correct (or equivalent), verifying buttons and status labels change per state
If incorrect submission is supported, submit an incorrect answer once and verify the UI provides feedback and allows retry
After completing practice items, verify Your progress card’s progress bar increases and stays consistent when switching problems or chat threads
exit_criteria: At least 3 practice problems completed across the panel with clear state transitions
Progress bar reflects completed items without regression during navigation within the page

phases.title: Settings/privacy flow via ⚙ + state persistence
phases.objective: Validate the primary settings/privacy entry point and confirm it behaves correctly (open/close, navigation, persistence, and accessibility), then re-check key flows after returning.
key_checks: Click ⚙ and verify a settings/privacy interface opens (dialog/panel/page section) with expected options or at minimum clear privacy-related controls
Test closing behavior (close button and Escape if applicable) and verify focus returns to the chat
If settings include toggles/checkboxes, change at least one and refresh/reload (or navigate threads) to confirm persistence if intended
Re-run a critical chat action after closing (send a message or toggle ▶ Practice) to ensure no UI is stuck in the wrong mode
exit_criteria: ⚙ settings/privacy UI is opened and closed successfully with no broken layout or trapped focus
At least one setting interaction is completed and its effect/persistence is validated

phases.title: Mobile viewport critical path checks
phases.objective: Repeat the most risk-prone interactions on mobile: tapping small controls, composer send, practice lifecycle, and settings/privacy access.
key_checks: Verify three-column layout collapses acceptably (rails become usable) and critical controls remain reachable
Tap ⚙ (small target) reliably; confirm settings/privacy opens and closes properly
Use composer: click into textarea and send a message; verify keyboard interactions and send button affordance on mobile
Complete at least one practice problem through Solve→Submit→Correct on mobile and confirm progress update
Tap 👍/👎 and Copy/Share once to ensure touch targets respond
exit_criteria: No blocking issues on mobile for settings/privacy, message sending, and at least one practice lifecycle
Touch interactions register (no accidental taps; no unresponsive controls)

coverage_targets.features: Exercise most visible controls per key page: subject clicks, chat thread switching, search, ⌥ Steps/▶ Practice/⋯ head tools, composer (textarea, Cmd+Enter, attach, mic, send), message tools (👍/👎/Share/Copy/Try again), and practice panel (Hint + Solve→Submit→Correct across multiple problems).
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat critical checks on mobile: ⚙ settings/privacy opening/closing, composer send, practice lifecycle completion, and feedback/copy/share touch responsiveness.

notes: Prescan only identifies index.html; settings/privacy likely manifests in-page via the ⚙ button, so prioritize validating that UI rather than searching for additional HTML pages.
Given small tap target warnings, spend extra steps on mobile for ⚙, ▶ Practice/⌥ Steps, and the 👍/👎/Copy controls to determine whether usability issues are purely theoretical or actually problematic.

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ✓ Executed from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ✓ Executed from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Correct 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Correct 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Submit 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 6 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule ·

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Correct 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Submit 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 5 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72

LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Submit 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Correct 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Correct 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 6 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule ·

Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. ✓ 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ✓ Executed from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Why is i² = −1? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Why is i² = −1?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Correct 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Correct 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Correct 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint C

It's the rate at which the inside is changing. observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ✓ Executed from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from. A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from., write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓

observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from. A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from., write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from. A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Show the chain rule on sin(3x) and explain where the 3 comes from., write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean!
